paragraphs: On the explication of the aspects of reflection upon the created things, and the bounty of God's beneficence upon them.

The author said: When we had set down in the First Gate the aspects of the purification of affirming the unity of God (mighty and exalted), and since reflection upon the manifest wisdom in the created things of the Creator (exalted be He) is the nearest of paths to verifying-the-reality of finding Him, and the most well-trodden of roads to the knowledge of His true reality, it was incumbent upon us to follow this with it — so that we might bring each gate together with what is fitting to it among the gates, and follow each concept with what befits it among the concepts by which there is laid upon us obedience to the Creator (exalted be He), for which He created us, as the Book says: "And God has so made it that men should fear before Him" (Ecclesiastes 3:14).

So I say first: the blessings of God (exalted be He) upon His creatures — though they be general and inclusive of all of them, as the Friend said: "The Lord is good to all, and His mercies are over all His works" (Psalms 145:9) — most of them are blinded from discerning these blessings, and from magnifying their worth. They are ignorant of their import on account of three obstacles.

**The first** is the great preoccupation with this world and the gathering of it, and their hunger after what has escaped them of it, and the failure of what they would have it yield them of its pleasures. So they look askance from reflection upon the blessings of God to themselves, on account of their souls' clinging to the great matter of what they hope for in the fulfillment of their appetites and the consummation of their hopes for it — for whenever they reach one station of it, they seek what is above it and crave what is beyond it. So they reckon the early blessings as too little, and slight the great gifts, until they take every blessing that has fallen to some other person as if it had been wrested from themselves, and what has accrued to them out of it as injuries that have struck them. They do not bring God to mind — the One who bestowed it upon them — like the saying of the Friend (peace be upon him): "The wicked man in his pride does not seek; 'There is no God' is the whole of his scheming" (Psalms 10:4).

**The second obstacle** is their emerging into this world while in the state of brutes — ignorant and unseeing — as the Wise One said: "Like a wild ass colt is man born" (Job 11:12); and their growing up amid the prior blessings of God and being constantly bound up with them, until those blessings become for them familiar and customary, as if they were essential to them — not separable from them, not parting from them all the length of their lives. So when they come to reason, and their discernment grows strong, they remain ignorant of the aspect of the blessing upon them, and do not bind their hearts to thank God for it, out of ignorance of the worth of the blessing and of the One who has bestowed it upon them.

Their case in this is like the case of a man of generosity who found an abandoned infant in a wasteland of the earth, and took pity on him, and brought him into his house, and raised him and fed him and clothed him and was lavish with him in every aspect of his welfare, until the child came to reason and understand the modes of his upbringing. Then this man heard of a captive in the hand of his enemy, who had reached an extreme of misery and hunger and nakedness over a long stretch of time — so he had compassion on his condition, and did not cease to manage matters gently with his enemy until he released him, and ransomed him at his price. Then, after this, the man brought him into his house and treated him kindly and was lavish with him in some part of what he had been lavish with upon the child. Then this captive man — once delivered — was more discerning and more grateful for the man's blessing upon him than the child who had been raised and brought up in his beneficence: because he had passed from the state of misery to the state of relief and ease in his moment of discernment, so that he was abundantly discerning of the kindness of the man of generosity to him and his bestowal of blessings upon him. The child, by contrast, was ignorant of the worth of the blessing upon him — even when his discernment grew strong and his reason was established — on account of his familiarity with it from the time of his infancy.

And no one of the people of reason doubts that the man's bounty and blessing upon the child were *greater*, and his beneficence to him *more manifest*, and the obligation of thanks and praise for it *more binding* — and this is what Scripture compares to in saying: "I myself taught Ephraim to walk, taking them in my arms; but they did not know that I healed them" (Hosea 11:3).

**The third obstacle** in their ignorance of the worth of God's blessing upon them is what befalls them in the world from the various kinds of injuries, and the various calamities that overtake them in their bodies and in their property. They are ignorant of the causes that lie behind the aspects of the blessing that are in these, and the benefits of trial and discipline for them within them — like the saying of the Friend (peace be upon him): "Happy is the man whom You discipline, O Lord, and out of Your Law do You teach" (Psalms 94:12). They forget that they themselves, and their property, are noble blessings God has bestowed upon them out of His generosity and bounty — that He then enacts among them, by His justice, what His wisdom has made obligatory; so they fall into despair at the going-forth of His justice among them, and they do not praise Him when His bounty and beneficence become manifest upon them.

So their ignorance carries them to denying the blessing and the One who has bestowed it — and in many of them the ignorance reaches so far as railing against Him in His deeds, and in the various creatures He has fashioned for their welfare.

How like they are, in this, to a company of blind men brought into a house prepared with everything for their welfare — every item set in the best position and most perfectly arranged, designed to deliver their benefits and aim at their welfare. Moreover, beneficial collyria were made ready for them in it, and a skilled physician to treat them with these collyria so that their sight might be restored — yet they were heedless of the treatment, and did not bind themselves to obedience to the physician set in charge of their cure. So they wandered about in the house, on the worst of conditions on account of their blindness; whenever they set out to walk in the house, they stumbled over the very arrangements set up for their welfare, and pitched forward upon their faces — some among them wounded, some broken. Great grew their misery, and their affliction redoubled. They turned to blaming the master of the house and the one who built it; they faulted his work and attributed to him deficiency and bad management; they claimed he had not aimed at their benefit and beneficence but rather at their misery and pain. This became the cause of their denial of the master of the house's blessing upon them, and of his beneficence to them — like the saying of the Wise One: "And even when the fool walks in the way, his heart is wanting, and he says to everyone, 'He is a fool'" (Ecclesiastes 10:3).

Since this is so, it is incumbent on the people of knowledge and understanding to awaken whoever is ignorant of God's blessings into discerning them, and to guide people to the knowledge of His bounty within them by the way of their intellects. For how many a blessing is its possessor deprived of its sweetness, and his joy in it spoiled, by his lack of discernment and his ignorance of its bounty! When the people of blessings are made to perceive the aspects of bounty in them, and there is unveiled to them what was hidden from them of these, great will be their praise and thanksgiving to the One who has bestowed them. There will come to them, by this, both the savoring of them in this world and abundant reward in the next, as the Wise One said in the matter of awakening: "The words of the wise are like goads, and as nails firmly fixed — the masters of collections; they were given by one Shepherd" (Ecclesiastes 12:11). He compares the speech of the wise, by way of awakening, to ox-goads; and likens it to firmly-fixed nails — for the gathering and binding-together and composing that they accomplish, to fix their meanings in the hearts, and the ordering of the aspects of wisdom by their means within the souls. And *baʿalei asuphot* was explicated as "masters of compilation," supplying the *divrei* from the start of the verse — so that the meaning reads: *and as nails firmly fixed are the words of the masters of compilation* — because books composed in the various kinds of wisdom are stable and enduring; their benefit is never severed. That is why he likens them to nails firmly fixed.
So it is now fitting that we explain, of the matter of reflection, six concepts:

1. The first: the definition of reflection and its true reality. 2. The second: whether we are obligated to reflect upon the created things or not. 3. The third: what is the manner of reflection upon the created things. 4. The fourth: how many kinds of wisdom there are in the created things by which we may reflect. 5. The fifth: which of the kinds is the nearest to us, and the most obligatory upon us to reflect upon, in preference to the rest. 6. The sixth: on the corrupters of reflection and their concomitants.

He said: As for the definition of reflection — it is the comprehension of the traces of God's wisdom (mighty and exalted) in the created things, and the registering of these in the soul according to the strength of the reflecting man's discernment.

For wisdom — though its traces vary in the created things — is one in its root and its source. It is like the sun, which is one in itself, but the colors of its ray differ in the panes of glass that are made of white glass, of green, of black, of red — so that its light differs according to the differences in the colors of the glass. And like the water by which the gardens are watered: it brings forth the flowers, differing in color, so that the water itself takes on color according to them. So understand, regarding the created things of the Maker (mighty and exalted) — both the small among them and the great — and consider attentively what is hidden from you of them, and you will find them as I have described, God willing.

It is on account of the difference of these traces in the created things that the comprehension and reflection upon them have been laid upon us — until their concept becomes established within our souls and settles in our imaginations. For if the traces of wisdom were uniform throughout all created things, no one would be in doubt regarding their matter, and the man of intellect and the ignorant would be equal in discerning them.

The cause for this — and God knows best and is wisest — on account of which not all created things were on a single pattern and a single shape, is that the thing that performs one action only, perpetually, indicates that its action is not by its choice — but rather it acts only by the nature with which it has been impressed, and there is a compeller compelling it to that action, with no possibility of changing it: like fire, whose action is only to burn; and like water, which cools only by its nature. But that which acts by its choice — diverse actions become manifest from it.

Since the Creator (exalted be He) is *choosing* in His action — not compelled, not constrained, not impressed-with-nature — He made the various things according to what His wisdom made obligatory, so that, by their variations, they might indicate His unity, and that He is choosing in His action — as the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "Whatever the Lord pleased, He did, in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and all the deeps" (Psalms 135:6). So the diversity of the traces of wisdom in the created things became necessary on this account. And His wisdom (exalted be He) is higher than that we should comprehend it — we have mentioned only one aspect from among many aspects we have not grasped, for to Him (mighty and exalted) belongs the perfect wisdom; there is no Lord besides Him.
He said: As for whether we are obligated to reflect upon the created things or not —
I say that reflection upon the created things, and inference by them concerning the wisdom of the Creator (mighty and exalted), is laid upon us by the rational, the scriptural, and the transmitted.

**As for the rational:** the intellect bears witness that the bounty of the rational over the non-rational is only by the bounty of its discernment, and its understanding, and its receptivity to knowledge — to the secrets of wisdom firmly fixed in the whole of the world — as the Book says: "Who teaches us by means of the beasts of the earth, and makes us wiser than the birds of the heavens" (Job 35:11). When a man employs his thought and his understanding in the secrets of wisdom and in reflection upon its traces, his bounty over the brute beast is according to that. But if he is heedless of them, he is like the brute beast — indeed, lower than it — as the Book says: "The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master's crib; Israel does not know, My people does not consider" (Isaiah 1:3).

**As for the scriptural:** the saying of the Book: "Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these?" (Isaiah 40:26). And the Friend said: "When I behold Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars which You have established" (Psalms 8:4). And the Book said: "Will you not know? Will you not hear? Has it not been told to you from the beginning? Have you not understood the foundations of the earth?" (Isaiah 40:21). And He said: "You deaf, hear, and you blind, look that you may see" (Isaiah 42:18). And He said: "Better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for that is the end of every man, and the living shall lay it to his heart" (Ecclesiastes 7:2). And He said: "The wise man's eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness" (Ecclesiastes 2:14). And He said: "The path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, shining ever brighter unto the established day; the way of the wicked is like darkness, they do not know in what they stumble" (Proverbs 4:18–19).

**As for the transmitted:** the saying of our early ones (peace be upon them): "Whoever is able to compute the cycles and the constellations and does not compute — concerning him Scripture says, *And the harp and the lyre, the tambourine and the flute and wine are at their feasts, but they do not look at the work of the Lord, and they do not see the doing of His hands*" (b. Shabbat 75a, citing Isaiah 5:12). And they said: "Whence that a man is obligated to compute the cycles and the constellations? As it is said: *And you shall observe and you shall do, for that is your wisdom and your understanding in the eyes of the peoples* (Deuteronomy 4:6) — what wisdom and understanding is there *in the eyes of the peoples*? — say: the computation of cycles and constellations" (b. Shabbat 75a). And they said: "Compute the loss of a commandment against its reward, and the reward of a transgression against its loss" (m. Avot 2:1). And they said: "Had the Torah not been given to Israel, we should have learned chastity from the cat, [aversion to] forbidden unions from the dove, propriety from the rooster, and not to rob from the ant" (b. Eruvin 100b).
The obligation of reflection upon the created things, and of inference by the traces of wisdom, has thus been established. Understand this.
He said: As for the manner of reflection upon the created things —

I say that reflection upon the created things is consideration of the pillars of the world, and of its branches composed of these, and of the disposition of the parts of every composite and the aspect of its utility, and of the traces of wisdom in its creation and its form and its shape and its welfare, and of the final cause for which it was created — and the discrimination between this world's spiritual aspect and its corporeal aspect, between its causes and its effects, its rational and its mute, its moving and its stationary, its solid and its growing, its higher and its lower. And [the recognition] that the Creator (exalted be He) composed the world by a firmly-knit composition, and arranged it by a tightly-binding arrangement, and parsed it by a clear parsing, and made it a pointer to Himself and an evidence for Himself — just as the craftsmanship indicates the craftsman, and the house the builder who built it.

You ought to know that the whole of the world is composed of corporeal entities and spiritual entities — they have been blended and mixed, and the one has come to be a vessel for the other, like the soul and the body in the living being.
The traces of wisdom in all of this are of three kinds.

**The first:** clear and manifest traces, hidden neither from the ignorant nor — all the more — from the man of intellect, such as the motion of the sun's sphere above the earth by day, to illuminate the inhabited zone so that creatures profit by it, as the Friend said: "When the sun rises, they gather themselves and crouch in their dens; man goes forth to his work and to his service until evening. How manifold are Your works, O Lord! In wisdom You have made them all" (Psalms 104:22–24).

**The second kind** of traces of wisdom: hidden from the creatures — the aspect of their rightness is known only by the man of intellect and understanding — like universal death for all human beings, in which there lies the welfare of the world, as our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "*And God saw all that He had made, and behold it was very good* (Genesis 1:31) — He means by this: behold, *death* is good" (Genesis Rabbah 9:5). And the Wise One said: "I praised the dead who are already dead, more than the living who are still living" (Ecclesiastes 4:2).

**The third kind** of traces of wisdom: manifest in one aspect and hidden in another — so that one of weak understanding cannot discriminate them except after careful investigation and inquiry. Such are the variations of universal conditions in the four seasons of the year and the like.

The skilled, sagacious one extracts from the world a knowledge of its spirituality and its subtleties, and makes them a ladder to inference about the Creator of the All (exalted be He) — and binds himself to obedience and worship of Him according to His majesty and greatness in his heart, and according to his discernment of the traces of His providence and His kindness to the whole of His creatures, and of His having preferred him with abundant blessings, and ennobled him over them, without any prior deed of his and without any prior excellence by which he might have earned the beautiful doing of God (exalted be He). Then he extracts from the corporeality of the world only that which carries benefit for his body and the maintenance of its state in this world — according to need and bare provisioning only — and leaves the rest of the world's superfluities and ornaments that distract the hearts from God (mighty and exalted), and strives in his action for his next world and for what he shall come to after his death. He holds the world and its goods to be a viaticum and a provision for his return and his next world; he takes from them only what will stand him in good stead when he sets out from them.

The one ignorant of the world and of the traces of wisdom within it makes it the house of his enduring and his dwelling-place; he strives for it with all his effort, and turns to it all his care and toil — supposing that he runs in the welfare of his own soul, not perceiving that his toil and the bounty of his amassings in it shall pass to another in his lifetime and after his death, while he himself has been wholly heedless of the matter of his next world.

How like these two are to two brothers who inherited from their father a piece of land that needed work and cultivation. They divided it into two halves; they had nothing besides it. One of them was intelligent and resolute, the other to the opposite. The intelligent one saw that occupying himself with his land alone would cut him off from contriving for his livelihood and procuring his sustenance, so he hired himself out in the working of another's land, that he might live from the wage of his work day by day. And whenever he was released from his work for another at the evening of his day, he seized his moment — an hour from it — and worked his land with diligence and energy. And whenever he had a surplus from his wages — of a day's sustenance or more — he left off working for another for that period, and worked his land with the utmost of his strength and energy. He continued so until he completed the work of his land in the most fitting manner; and when the time of its yield arrived and the season of its produce came, he gathered it and harvested it, and lived from it through the whole of his second year. He worked his land with intelligence, and never ceased increasing its yield until its produce sufficed for his sustenance — and there was a surplus left him, by which he could add to his land beyond his own.

But the ignorant brother — when he knew that working his land would cut him off from earning what would sustain him — abandoned it altogether and was heedless of it; and then he hired himself out to people in working land, took his wages, lived from them, and was sustained by them, but achieved nothing from them beyond his food and bare subsistence. When the food of his day was in surplus, he made of it a day of leisure and ease and recreation, and did not think of the matter of his land. He took his pleasure in the bathhouse in the times when there was surplus left him in his working-days. So his land remained idle, growing nothing — rather, thorns grew up on it, its hedges fell in ruin, and the torrents carried away its fruit — as the Wise One said: "I passed by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding; and lo, it was all grown over with thorns, the face of it was covered with nettles, and the stone wall of it was broken down" (Proverbs 24:30–31).

The intelligent man, when he sees this parable with his reason, reflects through it on the matters of his next world — which is his house in true reality — and works for it with all his diligence; and when he works for his this-world, he works for it as one who works in the land of another, only according to necessity and need. The ignorant one acts in the two matters to the opposite — he toils in the matters of his this-world and is heedless of the matters of his next world — like the saying of the Wise One in his reflection upon the ignorant man: "I beheld, and laid it to my heart; I saw and received instruction" (Proverbs 24:32).
As for how many kinds of traces of wisdom there are in the created things, by which we may reflect —
I say that the pillars of wisdom firmly fixed in the created things — for all the multiplicity of their kinds and individuals — are seven.

**The first:** the trace of the manifest wisdom in the roots and elements of the world — such as what we behold of the standing of the earth at the center, with water adjacent to it above, and air adjacent to water, and fire above that — all on a weight and a measure in which nothing alters: each one has been bound to the place specially marked for it, demarcated for it. The sea stands still — the water imprisoned within it — not transgressing its bound, even when its waves crowd together and its winds storm — as He said: "And I set My bound for it, and set bars and doors, and said: 'Thus far you shall come and no further; and here shall be set the proud-rising of your waves'" (Job 38:10–11). And He said of the standing of the earth and the sky: "Forever, O Lord, Your word is set firm in the heavens; from generation to generation is Your faithfulness; You have established the earth, and it stands fast. They stand this day according to Your judgments, for all are Your servants" (Psalms 119:89–91), and on the meaning that the Friend (peace be upon him) mentioned in the Psalm *Bless, O my soul* (Psalms 104).

**The second pillar:** the trace of the manifest wisdom in the species of the human being, who is the small world — by whom the perfection, order, beauty, ornament, and completion of this world come about, as the Friend (peace be upon him) explained in the Psalm *O Lord our Lord* (Psalms 8).

**The third pillar:** the trace of the manifest wisdom in the compositions of the human being — the assembly of his body, the powers of his soul, and the light of intellect with which God has singled him out and made him preferable to all the other animals that are non-rational. He is congruent to the great world and akin to it in his roots and his elements — and to this Job pointed in his saying: "Did You not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me with bones and sinews; life and beneficence You wrought with me, and Your visitation has preserved my spirit" (Job 10:10–12).

**The fourth pillar:** the trace of the manifest wisdom in the species of the rest of the animals — small and great — among them the flying, the swimming, the creeping, and the four-footed — in their differing varieties of forms, traits, dispositions, benefits, and welfare in the world, as is mentioned in God's description to Job, in His rebuke of him: "Who provides for the raven its prey?" (Job 38:41) — and the rest of what He described of the kinds of land animals and sea animals.

**The fifth pillar:** the trace of the manifest wisdom in plants and minerals, prepared for the welfares of the human being and the various kinds of his benefits within them — according to the differences of their natures, mixtures, and properties. The ancients in their books described some of this according to their apprehension — as the Book says: "And he spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that springs out of the wall" (1 Kings 5:13).

**The sixth pillar:** the trace of the manifest wisdom in the sciences, the crafts, and the activities by which God (great is His name) has inspired the human being for the completion of his welfare and the causes of his sustenance and the rest of his benefits, both general and particular. To these the Book has pointed in His saying: "Who has put wisdom in the inward parts, or who has given the rooster understanding?" (Job 38:36). And the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "For the Lord gives wisdom; from His mouth knowledge and understanding" (Proverbs 2:6).

**The seventh pillar:** the trace of the manifest wisdom in the institution of the religious laws and customs by which one obtains the means of voluntary devotion to God (mighty and exalted) — so that the one who binds himself to them attains, by them, the benefits of this world in the near term and the reward of the next world in the long term, as the Book says: "Listen diligently to Me, and eat what is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness. Incline your ear, and come to Me; hear, that your soul may live" (Isaiah 55:2–3). To this follows the various kinds of political governance by which the order of the management of the rest of the nations and their welfares is set — these standing in the place of the Law for matters of this world only. It has been said that the rank of nature in relation to the Law is like the rank of the slave in relation to his master: the natural powers run in the management of the world only according to what accords with the Law — as the Book says: "And you shall serve the Lord your God, and He will bless your bread and your water, and I will remove sickness from your midst" (Exodus 23:25); and He said: "And He said: If you will diligently hear the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is upright in His eyes, and give ear to His commandments, and observe all His statutes — every illness that I placed upon Egypt I shall not place upon you, for I am the Lord your healer" (Exodus 15:26). And many like this.
It may be that the Wise One's saying — "Wisdom has built her house, she has hewn out her seven pillars" (Proverbs 9:1) — intends these seven pillars that we have mentioned. Understand this.
As for which of the kinds is the nearest to us, and the most obligatory upon us to reflect upon —

I say that the reflection upon each one of them — though it be incumbent — is obligatory upon us; but the nearest of them to us, and the clearest in our view, is the trace of the manifest wisdom in the species of the human being, who is the small world, and who is the proximate cause for the existence of this world. So it is incumbent upon us to consider the human being's beginning and his coming-into-being, the composing of his parts and the structuring of his members, and the benefit conferred by each one of them, and the necessity that requires his being placed and shaped as he is. Then we should consider his welfare in each one of his traits and the powers of his soul, the light of his intellect, his substances and accidents, his hopes, and the end of his matter.

For when we stand upon what we have mentioned of the human being, much of the secret of this world becomes clear to us — for he is similar to it. Some of the philosophers have said that philosophy is *man's knowing of himself* — meaning by this the knowledge of what we have mentioned about the human matter, by which one may discern the Creator (mighty and exalted) from the trace of His wisdom in him, as in Job's saying: "And from my flesh I shall see God" (Job 19:26).

So it is fitting for us — if it be so — that we should mention, of all that we have described of the matters of the human being, a small portion from each concept that will rouse the heedless one to what he must remember always, and impel him to seek what I have not mentioned. So let him submit to his Creator on account of the magnitude of His favor to him and His beneficence toward him, and magnify his thanks to Him — as the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "I will give thanks to You, for I am awesomely set apart; wonderful are Your works, and my soul knows it well. My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret, intricately wrought in the depths of the earth; Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and in Your book all of them were written — days were fashioned, and not one of them" (Psalms 139:14–16).

So the first thing fitting for you, O my brother, is that you ascend by your thought to the beginning of the human and to the first inception of his coming-to-be. You will see that the first of God's blessings upon him is to bring him into existence after his non-existence — namely, his passing out of the rank of the elements into the rank of the plant, then his transferring from the rank of the plant into the rank of the nutriment, and from that to the rank of semen and blood, and then to the rank of the animal, and then to the rank of the human being — the speaking-rational mortal being. This proceeds by gradation, through transformations, by varied causes, by congruent intermediaries — composed by a perfected management and a firm order.

When you have reflected on this, and seen the trace of the generosity, the wisdom, and the power in the whole of it, reflect and consider the roots of his manifest composition — I mean his soul and his body. You will see the human body composed of mutually contrary elements and differing natures, which the Creator (exalted be He) brought together by His power and bound together by His wisdom, so that there came together from them a body — single and unified in its outward presentation, differing in its inner natures. Then He coupled with it a luminous, spiritual substance, congruent to the spirituality of the high beings — I mean by this substance the soul, which He has bound by intermediaries congruent to both extremes: namely, the animal spirit, the innate heat, the blood, the blood-vessels, the nerves, and the arteries. And He made for it causes that protect and preserve it and shield it from injuries — namely, the flesh, the bones, the muscle, the skin, the hair, the nails — all of them coverings and casings to protect it from injuries.

Then reflect, O my brother, on the subtlety of the Creator's management (mighty and exalted) of the human being. For He prepared for him his mother's womb at the start of his matter, so that he might be in the most secure of places and the most-walled of fastnesses, where no hand can reach him, where no heat or cold can come to him — with the firm wrapping and the well-fortified shelter, with the well-prepared nutriment. He never ceases growing and increasing until he has the strength to move and turn, with his nourishment ready to him without effort or trouble; for it has been prepared in such a place that no one of the human beings can arrive at conveying it to him by any of the means. Whenever the growth of his body increases, his nourishment grows in strength accordingly — until a fixed term. Then he comes forth from his mother's womb through the narrowest of paths, with no contrivance contrived for his being brought out, no kindly maneuvering used upon him to ease that for him — but only by the power of the One who is wise and gentle, the One who is pitying toward His servants — as God said to Job about some of the non-rational animals: "Do you know the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth? Do you watch the calving of the hinds? Can you number the months that they fulfill? And do you know the time when they bring forth?" (Job 39:1–2).

Then the infant is delivered into this world weak of senses — save the senses of taste and touch — and the Creator (exalted be He) prepares for him nutriment in his mother's breasts. The blood that was his food in his mother's belly is changed into milk in her breasts, flowing, sweet to drink, like a flowing spring at the hour of his need — not too much, lest it become a burden on his mother, flowing without his sucking; nor too little, lest it cause the infant misery in extracting and sucking it from the breast. And among the subtleties in this: that God (exalted be He) made the bore of the breast like the puncture of a fine needle — not wide, so that it might flow without his sucking, or choke the infant when he sucks at the breast; nor narrower than this, so that its extraction be difficult for the infant by sucking.

Then his body grows strong, so that he sees colors and hears sounds. And God casts pity and mercy into the hearts of his parents, so that they hold the raising of him to be easy, and prefer him to themselves in food and drink; and the burden and toil of his upbringing become light upon them — in washing him, cleaning him, dealing gently with him, and warding off injuries from him in spite of the infant's resistance.

Then he passes from the rank of infancy to the rank of childhood; and his parents do not weary of him, do not despair at the multitude of his calls and his slight discernment of what they bear of his coarseness and his expense and his trouble — rather, their concern and anxiety for him grows greater in their souls, until he reaches the full strength of his powers. He learns speech in order and gradation; the powers of his senses grow strong, and the powers of his soul, so that he becomes receptive to knowledge and understanding. He discriminates some sensible objects from others by means of his bodily senses, and some intelligible objects from others by means of his spiritual senses — as the Friend said: "For the Lord gives wisdom; from His mouth knowledge and understanding" (Proverbs 2:6).

And among the great blessings upon the human being is that in his state of infancy he does not reason and does not discriminate good and evil — for had his intellect and discernment been complete at his upbringing, so that he discriminated the bounty of people over him in their being self-sufficient, in the swiftness of their movement and their cleanliness — and saw his own state to the contrary — he would have died of grief and care and chagrin.

And among the wonders of his weeping is the infant's benefit by it, as the most excellent of the physicians claim — that in the brains of infants there is a moisture which, if left in its state, brings on them harmful effects; weeping dissolves that moisture from their brains, and they are kept safe from the evils that come from it. Then, among the great subtleties of the Creator's management (exalted be He) of the human being is the replacement of his teeth, one after another — so that eating may not become impossible for him through the length of time during which what has fallen from them is growing back.

Then sicknesses and painful accidents overtake him — so that he may discriminate himself from the world, and not be ignorant of its condition; lest he grow comfortable with it and his appetites for it master him, so that he becomes like the brute beast, neither reasoning nor understanding — and the Friend said: "Be not like the horse, like the mule, without understanding" (Psalms 32:9).

Then the human reflects with the sight of his heart, and considers the benefits of the members of his body and the aspect of his welfare in each member. The hands are for grasping and pushing; the feet for rising up; the eyes for seeing the way; the ears for hearing; the nose for smelling; the tongue for speech; the mouth for eating; the teeth for chewing; the stomach for digestion; the liver for purifying the nutriment; the channels for the discharge of the excess matter; the receptacles for carrying it; the heart, the dwelling of the innate heat and the spring of life; the brain, the dwelling of the spiritual powers and the spring of sensation, the root of the nerve; the genitals, for the upholding of the offspring. And so for the rest of the members of the body — and what is hidden from us of their benefits is more than what is manifest to us.

The like of this becomes evident to one who reflects on the inside of the body, and the operations of nature within it when the food enters and is divided to every part of the body's parts: he sees, of the traces of wisdom, what binds him to praise of his Creator and thanks to Him — as the Friend said: "All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like You?" (Psalms 35:10).

For the food passes to the stomach through a prepared channel on a straight line, with neither bend nor crookedness in it — namely the esophagus. Then the stomach grinds it more thoroughly than the first grinding which the molars performed; then it dispatches it to the liver in fine vessels that connect the two, which have been made like a strainer for the food, so that nothing coarse from it may reach the liver. The liver turns it into blood, divides it upon the body, and conveys it to all its parts in channels prepared for this — in the manner of the channels prepared for water. What remains of the residues passes to channels prepared for them: what is of the species of yellow bile flows to the bladder of bile; what is of the species of black bile flows to the spleen; what is of moisture and dampness flows to the lungs; what is of the running of blood flows to the bladder.

So reflect, O my brother, on the wisdom of the Creator (exalted be He) in the composition of your body and the placing of these members in their proper places, so that they may carry off those residues, and they not be spread through the body altogether and sicken it.

Then reflect on the forms of the instruments of voice and the places-of-articulation of speech: the larynx is like a tube for the issuing of the voice; the tongue, the two lips, and the teeth, for parsing the letters and the tones. And in these members are further benefits: in the larynx, breath passes to the lungs; by the tongue, tastes are tasted, and there is in it also aid for the swallowing of food and drink; by the molars the food is chewed; by the two lips the drink is sipped, so that what flows from them is by intention and measure — and so too in the rest of the members, the benefits of some of which are known to us and of some unknown.

Then reflect, O my brother, on the four powers in the body and their operations within it: **the attractive power** — which calls for the entry of the food and its arrival in the stomach; **the retentive power** — which holds the food and keeps it in the stomach until nature performs its work upon it; **the digestive power** — which cooks it, extracts its pure essence, and disperses it through the body; **the expulsive power** — which sends down the leftover residue once the digestive power has taken what it needs from the food.

Look how these powers have been deputed in the body for its maintenance in what makes for its rightness. They are in the place of a house of a king, in which there are servants and stewards charged with the upkeep of the house. One is charged with making the requests of the servants and conveying them to the king's storehouse-keeper; a second steward receives what the first delivers and stores it in the house until it is ready and put right; a third steward is for the treatment of what has been stored, putting it right, preparing it, and distributing it among the servants; and a fourth steward sweeps from the house the filth and the dirt and clears it out.
Then reflect on the powers of the soul and how they bear on the benefits of the human being — such as thought, memory, forgetting, shame, intellect, and speech.

Were the human being to be deprived of memory alone among these traits — what would his state become? How many defects would befall him in his matters? — he would not remember what he had taken and what he had given, what he had seen and what he had heard, what he had said and what had been said to him; he would not recall the one who treated him well or the one who treated him ill, what benefited him from what harmed him; and he would not be guided to a road even if he had traveled it many times; he would not retain knowledge though he should have studied it the length of his life. He would not benefit from experience, nor measure a thing against what has passed, nor what shall be against what has been — rather, it would be fitting that he be stripped from humanity altogether.

And among the qualities of forgetting: were it not for it, no one would be consoled for a calamity, nor would any of the world's joys distract him from it, nor would he take delight in what gladdens him when he recalled the world's misfortunes — nor would there be hope of relief from one who envies him, or respite from one who rules over him.
Do you not see how He placed in the human both memory and forgetting — though they be opposites and contraries — and made for him in each of them aspects of welfare?

Then reflect on the trait of shame with which He singled out the human: how great is its worth, how vast its benefit and its welfare! Were it not for it, a guest would not be honored, a promise would not be kept, needs would not be supplied, the good thing would not be accomplished, the ugly thing not avoided in anything — to the point that many of the matters of the Law are imposed only on account of shame. For most of the people, were it not for shame, would not regard the rights of their fathers, much less of others; nor would they hand over what was entrusted to them; nor would they hold back from a foul deed. The one who does any of what we have mentioned does so only after he has thrown off the cloak of shame, as the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed they have done shamefully and feel no shame; they do not even know how to be ashamed" (Jeremiah 6:15); and He said: "The wrongdoer knows no shame" (Zephaniah 3:5).

And among the wonders, O my brother, is that He has bestowed upon the human shame before people for the benefits we have described, and for what is greater than what our description has comprehended — but He did not place in his nature shame before God (mighty and exalted), who is ever watching over him. For if [shame before God] had been a matter of his nature, he would have been compelled to obey Him, and the aspect of his earning the reward of his obedience would have been weakened. But shame before God is incumbent upon us by the way of reflection, and by our knowledge of what is incumbent upon us toward Him of obedience, and by our knowledge that He is gazing upon our outward and our inward — as His saying: "Be ashamed and humiliated for your ways, O house of Israel" (Ezekiel 36:32).

As for the great blessing of God (mighty and exalted) upon us in the intellect and discernment with which He has singled us out beyond all the rest of the species of the human family — the benefit of this is not hidden from us in the management of our bodies and the order of our motions, [as contrasted with] those of us who have been deprived of this by some accident befalling the brain.

The qualities that come to us on account of the intellect are very many. Among them: by it we infer that we have a Creator — wise, sole, eternal, singular, eternal-without-beginning, powerful — who is contained by no time and no place; majestic beyond the descriptions of the creatures; exalted beyond the imaginations of the existents; merciful, generous, lavish, who resembles nothing and whom nothing resembles. By it, also, we have come to understand the wisdom, the power, and the mercy diffused throughout the world, and the obligation of obedience to Him and the worship of the One who is worthy of it — by reason of His blessings, general and particular. By the intellect the Book of God becomes valid for us — the truthful one, revealed by Him to His messenger (peace be upon him), with which He laid us under obligation. According to the measure of the man's intellect and discernment falls the reckoning and the demand upon him from God (exalted be His mention). The one who is deprived of his intellect — the qualities of being human fall from him altogether, along with their burdens, their rewards, and their punishments.

Among the qualities of the intellect: by it the human apprehends all his sensible and intelligible objects of apprehension; by it he sees what is hidden from his bodily senses among visible things — like the moving of a shadow, and the effect of a single drop of water upon hard rock. By it he parses between the true and the false, between the excellent and the deficient, between the good and the evil, between the beautiful and the ugly, between the necessary, the possible, and the impossible. By it he subdues the rest of the species of the animal for his welfare and his benefit. By it he discriminates the places of the stars and their distances, the motions of the spheres, the proportions and geometrical measures, the forms of logical proofs, and the rest of the sciences and crafts whose mention would prolong us. So also, the rest of the human's traits, when you reflect upon them, you will find at the utmost of welfare and benefit for him — like what we have described in the case of the intellect.

Then reflect on what God has bestowed upon the human in speech and the order of utterance, by which he expresses what is in his soul and his inward, and understands from another. The tongue is the pen of the heart, the interpreter of the soul, the envoy of the inward; and were it not for speech, the human's company with those he companions would be severed, and he would be as the brute beast. By speech the disparity between people becomes manifest, and by it covenants are bound between them, and between them and God and His friends. By speech slips are made good, sins are sought forgiveness; and it is the strongest evidence for people's excellences and their vices. It has been said: *the human is just the heart and the tongue* — and by this the definition of the human is perfected, I mean by speech, since the definition of the human is *the speaking-rational mortal living being*; and by it he is parsed off from the brutes.

Then reflect on the bounties of the marks of writing and inscription — by which the traces of the past and the present are recorded for those who come after, and by which the reports of the absent are conveyed to the present, and the states of travelers to their relatives — through whose transmittal sometimes their lives and their deliverance from disasters and destructions depend. By it the sciences are made eternal in books; by it the meanings scattered in [men's] hearts are ordered; by it people record what has gone on between them by way of dealings, trade, debt, the buying of land, marriage-contract, divorce, manumission — and the matter is greater than we can encompass.

And among the perfection of blessings to the human in it: He has prepared for him a palm and fingers by which he masters drawing, writing, inscribing, the [making of] sparks for fire, and the rest of subtle activities and crafts — apart from the other species of the human animal, since these have no need of them.

I say: there is no member whose aspects of benefit I have mentioned but that the traces of wisdom in its composition, placement, and joining are manifest to whoever has comprehended them; these are powerful witness, clear in their indication, of the Creator's providence (exalted be He) toward us. Galen has set out for us in his book *The Benefits of the Members* an eloquent exposition; and were we to set ourselves to the exposition of this in a single member, the discourse would carry us beyond the limit of intent. In what we have brought, there is some awakening for one who has been guided to what holds his salvation, God willing.

As for reflection on the rest of the kinds of animals, their management and their sustenance — this is not hidden from one who reflects upon them and comprehends the traces of wisdom in them. That is why you see the Book repeatedly mentioning them when it recounts the wonders of the Creator (exalted be He) — what He said to Job: "Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry to God?" (Job 38:41); and He said: "He gives to the beast its food, to the young ravens which cry" (Psalms 147:9), and many like it.

Likewise, when you look upon the diverse running of the spheres in diverse motions and diverse lights, by which the state of the whole is ordered, you will see, of the traces of power and wisdom, what no human imagination can comprehend, and what the tongue is powerless to describe — as the Friend said: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament tells of the work of His hands" (Psalms 19:2), and the rest of the Psalm; and He said: "When I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars which You have established" (Psalms 8:4).

And among the most wondrous of the great created things on which the human eye may fall is the sky. For wherever he stands on the earth, he sees half of the sphere that encompasses the earth. When the one looking at it looks reflectively, he sees that the One who created it by His will is unending in His power, His wisdom, and His majesty. For when we are shown some trace of an ancient building of an early people, we marvel at their power to do its like — it indicates to us the strength of their bodies and the loftiness of their ambition in fortifying themselves. If this small look and this slight trace looms so large in our eyes — though it does not exceed our own work except by a little — how much more must we hold in awe the Creator of the earth and the sky and what is between them, without burden, without trouble, without weariness, without fatigue — not from anything, not upon anything, not by means of anything, but by His will and His wish — as it is said: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of His mouth all their host" (Psalms 33:6).

And among the totality of blessings upon the human: whenever you reflect on the traces of wisdom in the created things, you find them — along with their witness to the Creator (exalted be He) for lordship and unity — never separate from an aspect of benefit and an intent for welfare for the human being, save that some of them are manifest and some hidden. Among these are light and darkness: the benefits of light are evident and manifest, not hidden. As for darkness, its benefits are hidden — because of people's loneliness within it, and the cutting-off of their works and movements at its falling. Yet were it not for the darkness of night, the bodies of most animals would have been cut off by the continuity of their labor, the persistence of their work, and the length of their motion. By night, one part of time is parsed off from another; by it the unknown stretches of time and the length and shortness of terms are determined. And were the state always upon one form, there would have been no Law containing in itself time — like the Sabbath, the festival, the fast — and there would be no promise among people up to a fixed time; and ignorance of most of the things contained in time; and the digestion of food in the stomach of any animal would not have been complete.

Since the human had need of light by night to do some of his works in it — and to be cheered by it in his sickness — God compensated him with the light of fire, to employ it by night whenever he wills and extinguish it whenever he wills.

And among the wonders is that the color of the sky is what strengthens the eye — I mean: inclining toward black. It is among its properties that it concentrates and strengthens vision; were it white, it would harm the eye of the animal and weaken the strength of the eye. And so it is for the secret of wisdom in the rest of the created things.

And among the great blessing of God upon the human: that he is feared by the rest of the harmful animals, as the Book said: "Your fear and your dread shall be upon every beast of the earth" (Genesis 9:2) — to the point that the infant is safe from the cat and the rat and the like; and when a man dies, he is not safe from what we have mentioned of the animal — as our early ones (peace be upon them) said: "A one-day-old infant — alive, he does not need to be guarded from the mice; Og king of Bashan — dead, he must be guarded from the mice. As it is said: *Your fear and your dread shall be upon every beast of the earth*" (b. Shabbat 151b).

And among what is fitting for you to comprehend from the whole of created things — their high and their low, their small and their great — is the hidden concept by which the system of the whole and its perfection holds: it is not apprehended by the bodily senses. It is the motion that necessarily attaches to every composite; no sense among the bodily senses apprehends it. The intellect apprehends it only by the mediation of the moving thing, which the senses do apprehend. Were it not for motion, the coming-to-be of any of the existent things would not have been completed, nor their corruption. Some of the philosophers have said: *the spirit of natures is motion*.

When you have understood the secret of motion, and grasped the concept of its true reality and its spirituality, and known that it is among the subtleties of divine wisdom; and discriminated the strength of the Creator's providence (exalted be He) over creation — then you will become verified-of-the-reality that all your motions are bridled by the will of the Creator (exalted be He), and His management, and His wish — the small and the great of them, the hidden and the manifest — save what He has entrusted to you of the choice of obedience or transgression. When you have verified-of-the-reality of this, examine your soul at every motion you move with, and remember God's bridle (mighty and exalted) upon you in it; and bind yourself to shame before Him, and to watchful awareness of Him, and to submission to His judgment — be satisfied with His decree, and you shall arrive at His satisfaction, and the outcome of your matters shall be made beautiful — as the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "And the one who trusts in the Lord — kindness shall encompass him" (Psalms 32:10).

And among the matters of the world upon which it is fitting that you reflect is the careful observation of the outcomes of matters that are made difficult and easy for us. You will see therein an astonishing wonder, for many a thing that befalls us with vexation — its outcome we shall praise, and the opposite. It has been said that some travelers slept by the foot of a wall; a dog came and urinated on one of them, so he rose to his feet to wash himself of the urine; when he had moved far from his companions, the wall collapsed upon them and they died, and he was saved. And again, that a man was walking in a caravan and had need of relieving himself; he moved far from it and answered his need; he was at the edge of the road, and when he had finished, he fell asleep without intending to. He awoke after an hour, was dismayed, and regretted his sleep; he set out in pursuit of the caravan, hoping to catch up with it. He caught up with it at the place where he had parted from it — and behold, it had been slaughtered: bandits had fallen upon it, and despoiled it, and killed them. Many things like this and the opposite occur.

And among the greatest of what is fitting that you reflect upon: the universality of sustenance for the animal of the earth and its plants — like the rains in their time of need and their falling in their seasons — as the Book says: "Are there any among the vanities of the gentiles that can cause rain? Or can the heavens give showers? Are You not He, O Lord our God? We hope in You" (Jeremiah 14:22). And He said: "They did not say in their hearts: Let us now fear the Lord our God, who gives the rain — the former rain and the latter rain — in its season, who keeps for us the appointed weeks of the harvest" (Jeremiah 5:24). The Book magnifies the matter of it greatly in its saying: "Who does great things beyond searching out, wonders without number, who gives rain upon the face of the earth, and sends water upon the face of the fields, to set up on high those that are low, and those that mourn for safety are exalted" (Job 5:9–11).

And among the wonders, of the causes of foods from the grains, is that a single grain bears a thousand grains and more, if it is preserved from injuries. It has been said that there is found in a single grain of wheat three hundred ears, and in every ear more than twenty grains of wheat — in some places. We find the great fruits whose root is a single seed and whose growth is from one — at the analogy of multiplication I have mentioned. Glory be to the Wise One, the Sustainer, who appoints great things to come about from the subtlest of causes and the weakest of them — as the Book says: "And actions are weighed" (1 Samuel 2:3).

As for the particularities of the sustenance for the individuals among the species of the animal — that is more than our description can encompass. The skilled one, when he reflects upon them and grasps their causes, discriminates from them the wisdom of the Creator's management within them — and concerning them the Friend says: "They all wait for You, that You may give them their food in its time. You give to them, they gather; You open Your hand, they are satisfied with good" (Psalms 104:27–28). And He said: "You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing's desire" (Psalms 145:16). I shall enlarge upon this matter in the Gate of Reliance on God, God (exalted be He) willing.

And among the greatest of blessings God has bestowed upon the human, and the strongest in indication of Him, is the Law revealed to the Messenger (peace be upon him); and the appearing of the signs by his hand, and the breaking-of-the-ordinary, and the altering of natures, and the showing-forth of miracles — for the verifying of the Creator and the certainty of His messenger — as it is said: "And Israel saw the great hand which the Lord did against the Egyptians, and the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord and in Moses His servant" (Exodus 14:31); and He said: "You have been shown to know that the Lord is God, there is none other besides Him" (Deuteronomy 4:35); and He said: "Out of the heavens He made you hear His voice, that He might discipline you; and upon the earth He made you see His great fire, and you heard His words out of the midst of the fire" (Deuteronomy 4:36).

If, in our time, anyone seeks the like of these traces — let him look with the eye of fairness at our state among the nations from the time of the exile, the ordering of our matters among them, despite our being against them in secret and openly, and their knowledge of this from us; he will see that our state, perhaps, has equaled their state in foods and sustenance, and perhaps our state has been better than theirs in times of war and dissension — so that you see [the nations'] peasantry and the lowly populace of their countryside more miserable by far than our middle ones and our lowliest. This is on the strength of the assurance the Creator (exalted be He) has given us: "And yet, even when they are in the land of their enemies, I shall not despise them, nor shall I abhor them" (Leviticus 26:44); and Ezra said: "Though we are slaves, yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery" (Ezra 9:9); and the Friend said: "If it had not been the Lord who was for us, let Israel now say — when men rose up against us…" (Psalms 124:1–2), and the rest of the Psalm. I shall expand in the Gate of Binding-Oneself-to-Obedience-to-God on the mention of the bounty of His blessing upon us in the Law He laid down for us — what shall suffice, God willing.

And among what is fitting should occur to your mind — and you should reflect on it — is the gathering of the word of the multitude of the people and the binding-together of their hearts, despite the great difference of their dispositions, by the placing-forward of one man among them whom they obey: they pause at his command and his prohibition, hold his power in awe — so he preserves them, has compassion on them, is just among them, brings them upon what is the rightness of all of them, so that their affairs do not fall to ruin, and the enemy does not prevail over them. Were each of the people to look to himself for the defending of himself, they would not agree upon the building of a fortress or a wall, and their conditions would be lost.

Together with this, the friend over the people — with his management of them — preserves the impressions of the Laws, and brings the people upon the just customs and the traces of the excellent beauty: he is the servant of the Law and the keeper of just polity — by these two his matter is stable and his kingship endures, as it is said: "Kindness and truth preserve the king" (Proverbs 20:28); and our early ones said: "Pray for the welfare of the kingdom, for were it not for the fear of it, every man would swallow his fellow alive" (m. Avot 3:2).

And among what is fitting for you, O my brother, that you reflect upon and comprehend of the traces of high wisdom and consummate providence: people's convention to buy and sell with silver and gold, and their striving to accumulate them — a subtle gift of God to them, so that by these two the maintenance of their state may stand. Yet need is not satisfied by these in themselves: for he who is overtaken by the pain of hunger and thirst, lacking food and water — the abundance of these does not benefit him, nothing of them avails him. Likewise, if there is pain in one of his members, he is not treated with silver or gold. Indeed, many other minerals are used in many kinds of treatment — and seldom does it happen by silver or gold.

It is on this account that you see them in abundance among the people from the angle that they are never without them — but they are scarce with most of them: had they been existent in abundance among all of them, no need of theirs would have been met by them. So they are scarce in one respect, abundant in another; likewise they are precious in one respect, contemptible in another, since there is no benefit in them by themselves — and this is among the highest of the management of high wisdom for them.

Then look, after this, at the matters by which the maintenance of bodies and their abiding in their state and their growing to the term of their lives are sustained. You will find them, in abundance and scarcity, according to the strength of the need for them. The stronger the need for a thing is, the more readily-found and existing it is; the more endurance and patience are possible for a thing, the harder it is to find and the rarer in being. The example of this: since one cannot endure without the air one breathes — even for an hour or more, in any way — the Creator (mighty and exalted) brought it into existence in the world and made it readily-available, so that it is not impossible for anyone, wherever he be, at any time and in any place. As for water — though it be needed like the air, except that endurance without it is more possible than without air — the Creator (exalted be He) released it upon the face of the earth, and gathered it in a particular place to which animals can go: it is not impossible for them, except that it is not in every place as the air is; and for most of the people it is sought-out at a price, which is not the case for air. It is available to some of the animals more than to others, while the air is equal in being-found and in apprehension by all of them, always in one state.

Then, since food too is needed — except that endurance without it, and substitution for it, are more possible than for air or water by far — its apprehension is more difficult and its being-found is rarer than water by far. Yet, in spite of this, it is abundantly existent, not absolutely impossible to people. And likewise the causes of clothing — out of furs and growth-products — are rarer than food, and slower in apprehension save after a stretch of time, on account of the possibility of endurance without them, and of subsistence on a little of them for a long stretch of time, more than with food.

As for precious stones, silver, gold, and the rest of the minerals: since they are of lesser need in themselves and remoter benefit — except by convention upon them — there is not found of them, with the multitude of the people, what is found of food with one of them. That is on account of the cause I have described, of being-without-need-of-them. Glory be to the Wise Creator, the Subtle in relation to His servants, the Merciful upon them, severe in providence for their welfares — there is no god save Him — as it is said: "You spared the gourd, for which you did not labor and which you did not raise; and I — shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city?" (Jonah 4:10–11); and the Friend (peace be upon him) said: "The Lord is good to all, and His mercies are over all His works" (Psalms 145:9).
He said: As for the corrupters of reflection and their concomitants —

I say that the totality of the corrupters of *tawḥīd* whose mention preceded in the First Gate — all of these are corrupters of reflection. The three obstacles we mentioned at the head of this gate are also among the totality of its corrupters. And among them is wonderment at the blessings of God (mighty and exalted) — so that the ignorant, the dim-witted, supposes that he is worthy of them and of what is greater than they; he does not reflect on the blessings of God, nor bind upon himself thanks and praise to the Creator for them. Concerning his like the Wise One said: "Every one proud of heart is an abomination to the Lord" (Proverbs 16:5).

As for the concomitants of reflection: of these is the human's collecting of God's blessings upon him, and his binding-himself-to-obedience on account of them; and of these is the human's perpetually turning over the traces of the Creator's wisdom (exalted be He) in his own soul — so that he is never empty of cogitation upon them and inquiry into them in everything that comes upon him among sensible and intelligible objects. He never ceases to see a new trace each day, as the Friend said: "Day unto day pours forth speech" (Psalms 19:3).

And among the totality of what is fitting for you to know, O my brother, when you read what I have awakened you to in this gate, is that it is little of much — much of what you may reach by your understanding of the secrets of wisdom, when you have uncovered them by purity of your inward and clarity of your heart. When you have reached, from this, the utmost that is in your power, it is fitting that you know that all you have stood upon of the wisdom of the Creator (exalted be He) and His power in this world is no portion of His power and His wisdom: for there is manifest of it only that to which necessity calls — on account of the human alone, not according to the possibilities of His power, for that has no end.

So let there be in your soul, of His majesty and the fear of Him and the magnitude of His power, according to this — not according to what you understand of Him alone. Rather, your own example in the world is like a child born in the king's dungeon: the king attended to his matter, and commanded for him all of his welfares, and dealt subtly with him until he grew up and reasoned. He has no knowledge of anything but the dungeon and what is in it. The king's messenger used to come back and forth to him with all that he needed of lamp and food and drink and clothing; and he made known to him that he is the king's servant, and that the dungeon, with all it contains and with all the food the messenger brings to it, belongs to the king. Then [the messenger] bound him to thanking and praising him; so he said: "Glory be to the master of this dungeon, who has made me his servant, and singled me out by the whole of his blessings, and made me his concern and his occupation."

The messenger said to him: "Why do you speak so? You err! For this dungeon alone is not the kingdom of the king. In the breadth of his lands are dungeons like this — innumerable in multitude. So too, you are not his servant alone — for his servants are more than can be numbered. And likewise: what you have experienced of his blessing and his bounty has no measure compared to his blessing upon others; and likewise his occupation with your matter has no measure compared to his occupation with what is besides you."
The child said: "I have no knowledge of what you have mentioned. I have understood the matter of the king only according to what I have experienced of his kingship and his blessing — only that."

The messenger said to him: "Say: *Glory be to the lofty King, whose kingship has no end, no limit to His blessing and His bounty; no measure for me amid the magnitude of His armies, no value for my matter amid the majesty of His power, glorious is He*."

The child understood, from the matter of the king, what he had been ignorant of; magnified his power in his own soul; held his command in awe; reckoned his blessing great, and what had come to him from the king's side, on account of the greatness of His estate; reckoned the value of the child within his kingdom slight, and his gifts abundant.

And you, O my brother, are the like of this regarding the sphere encompassing the earth — for we do not reason what is in the least patch of the earth, much less the whole of it, much less what is beyond the sphere. So comprehend, O my brother, this parable, and reflect by it; and grasp the concept of the Creator (mighty and exalted) according to this — so that there grow great within your soul that with which He has graced you of His blessings and bounties in His regard for you among the totality of His created things. Look upon His Book, His command, and His prohibition with the eye of His majesty; and bring before your mind the magnitude of your fread and your reverence for whatever may come to you of a blessing from the one above you among people — for according to the measure of the bounty of his rank above your rank, and his freedom-from-need-of-you, will be the measure of the majesty of his blessing in your soul. So likewise it shall be, for His command and His prohibition, according to that — a measure in your soul, in your striving, and in your effort for Him. So comprehend and understand — you shall hit the mark, God willing.
May God set us and you among those granted success in His obedience, those who discriminate the various kinds of His blessing — by His mercy and His pity, exalted is He.
